Apple today officially challenged a civil contempt ruling against it, filing its merits brief with the US Supreme Court in its years-long legal battle with Epic Games. Here's the full rundown.

Quick background

9to5Mac readers know the Supreme Court recently granted Apple's petition to review a civil contempt ruling stemming from Epic Games' lawsuit against Apple that began in 2020.

Quick recap: while Apple won on most of Epic Games' original claims, it lost on one key issue: the court ruled that Apple's "anti-steering" rules violated California's Unfair Competition Law.

As a result, the court issued a permanent injunction requiring Apple to let developers add links and other calls to action that direct users to third-party payment options.

That injunction reads:

Apple modified its rules to allow these links, but charges a commission of up to 27% on transactions completed through them. When Epic challenged Apple's compliance plan, the court sided with the Fortnite maker, ruling Apple had violated the injunction and was in civil contempt.

Today's brief

In today's brief, Apple pointed out that "when Apple submitted its notice of compliance on January 16, 2024, the district court raised no immediate objection."

Apple further noted that Epic itself acknowledged that the injunction "did not explicitly prohibit" Apple from charging a commission on transactions completed outside of the App Store. Despite this, Epic argued the new commissions and related rules violated the "spirit" of the injunction, with the district court agreeing.

Apple has been trying to get the civil contempt ruling overturned ever since, arguing that nothing in the original injunction prohibited it from charging commissions. That ruling is what Apple is now asking the Supreme Court to overturn.

Apple filed its opening brief today laying out its arguments in detail for why the civil contempt ruling should be thrown out.

Apple argued that "civil contempt sanctions may not be imposed for violation of an order unless the order clearly states that the action is prohibited," citing past court rulings that support its argument, noting that "a party may not be held in contempt unless the order leaves no reasonable doubt that the specific conduct was prohibited."

From the brief:

Apple also pushed back on the broader Ninth Circuit standard, arguing that the appeals court's allowance for civil contempt based on violating the "spirit" of an injunction is an outlier. Apple argued this allows courts to retroactively decide that certain behavior was prohibited, even if the injunction itself never explicitly said so.

Apple also argued that upholding the civil contempt ruling would open up the risk of judicial overreach by courts when enforcing injunctions:

With Apple's merits brief now filed, Epic will have until November 13 to file its response, and Apple's reply brief will be due December 14. The case could be heard by the Supreme Court as early as January 2027.
